| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.

Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05

author: Clankerusecase

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents

| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Hacker News
2026-07-25 13 use cases 8 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

For years, phishing campaigns targeting financial institutions followed the same playbook. Victims were tricked into entering usernames and passwords, attackers collected the credentials, and accounts were compromised later when an opportunity arose. That model is changing. Recent investigations into insurance-focused phishing operations reveal a more immediate approach. Instead of harvesting

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] InsureTrap malvertising: Google Ads referrer landing on free-hosting insurance phish · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] InsureOTP kit exfiltration: browser connecting to api.telegram.org Bot API · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
InsureTrap malvertising: Google Ads referrer landing on free-hosting insurance phish AIDelivery Medium
Hunts corporate users who reach a credential-harvesting page hosted on the disposable platforms CTM360 named for the InsureTrap campaign (GitHub Pages, Netlify, Wix, Hostinger, Lovable) via a Google Ads click referrer. This is the campaign's signature initial-access chain: sponsored 'compare car insurance' ads redirecting to look-alike insurer portals on free hosting rather than email/SMS lures. Rationale: Uses the exact delivery vector (Google Ads referrer) and the specific free-hosting platforms CTM360 named for InsureTrap (GitHub Pages/Netlify/Wix/Hostinger/Lovable). Referrer+host on a single proxy row is high-signal; endpoint fallback uses a 90s ad-click->landing correlation. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because HTTP referrer is not carried in FDR DNS/network or the standard Datadog sources. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ctm360.com/reports/insuretrap-fake-insurance-phishing-account-hijacking • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ctm360-research-reveals-how-insurance.html
ATT&CKT1583.008 T1566.002 T1204.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate small-business insurance broker whose real site is hosted on Netlify/Wix and advertised via Google Ads
  • Marketing landing pages your own org hosts on GitHub Pages/Netlify reached through a Google Ads campaign
  • SaaS product demo/preview sites on lovable.app or netlify.app that users find via sponsored search
  • Ad-tech redirectors that pass a doubleclick referrer to any downstream site the user browses next
Suppression filter
| where not (Url has_any ("<your-corp-brand>.netlify.app","<your-corp-brand>.github.io"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the landing Url and referrer; confirm the host is a randomized subdomain with insurance branding (logo/quote workflow) impersonating a known insurer rather than a legitimate business site. 2) Contain: block the specific host/FQDN at the web proxy and DNS, and warn/reset any user who submitted credentials or an OTP on the page. 3) Hunt: pivot on SrcUsername/DeviceId for a follow-on connection to api.telegram.org (see the Telegram exfil UC) and for repeat visits to sibling randomized subdomains on the same free-hosting platform.
let Window = 90s;
let AdClicks = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("googleadservices.com","googleads.g.doubleclick.net","g.doubleclick.net")
    | project DeviceId, AdTime = Timestamp;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("github.io","netlify.app","netlify.com","wixsite.com","hostingersite.com","lovable.app","lovableproject.com","lovable.dev")
| join kind=inner AdClicks on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (AdTime .. AdTime + Window)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, LandingUrl = RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, AdTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, AdTime)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("github.io","netlify.app","netlify.com","wixsite.com","hostingersite.com","lovable.app","lovableproject.com","lovable.dev")
| where HttpRequestHeaderReferer has_any ("googleadservices.com","doubleclick.net","googleads")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, HttpHostName, Url, Referer = HttpRequestHeaderReferer, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

InsureOTP kit exfiltration: browser connecting to api.telegram.org Bot API AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a browser process making an outbound connection/DNS lookup to api.telegram.org — the Bot API host the InsureOTP kit uses to relay harvested credentials and OTP codes to operators in real time. Legitimate Telegram web clients talk to web.telegram.org/Telegram DCs, not the Bot API host, so a browser reaching api.telegram.org is a strong client-side phishing-exfil indicator. Rationale: api.telegram.org is the concrete Bot API host CTM360 tied to the InsureOTP kit's exfiltration, corroborated as a phishing-kit exfil channel by Securelist and the SOCFortress FEMITBOT writeup. Browser-initiated traffic to it (vs. web.telegram.org for legit clients) is inherently anomalous, giving a low-FP alerting-grade signal. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/telegram-phishing-services/109383/ • https://socfortress.medium.com/the-telegram-trap-inside-the-sophisticated-femitbot-fraud-network-8b310c8c9df8 • https://www.ctm360.com/reports/insuretrap-fake-insurance-phishing-account-hijacking
ATT&CKT1567 T1102 T1111
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer testing a legitimate Telegram bot from a browser-based API console or Swagger/Postman-in-browser session
  • Internal IT/marketing automation dashboards that embed Telegram Bot API calls and are opened in a browser
  • Browser extension that legitimately integrates a personal Telegram bot for notifications
  • Security researcher or this very hunt loading api.telegram.org documentation/endpoints in a browser
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("dev-automation-host", "marketing-notify-host")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the tab/URL that drove the connection and whether the initiating browser had just loaded a free-hosting insurance page (correlate with the InsureTrap malvertising UC on the same device/user). 2) Contain: force-reset the user's credentials and revoke sessions for any insurer/personal accounts entered, and block api.telegram.org egress for standard user browsers at the proxy. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for browser->api.telegram.org, extract the visited phishing host from proxy logs, and block sibling randomized domains; check whether harvested identity data (policy/ID documents) warrants fraud/notification workflows.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.telegram.org"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Conns = count(), any(RemoteIP) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl
| order by LastSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DnsQuery =~ "api.telegram.org" or DnsQuery endswith ".api.telegram.org"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Lookups = count() by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery
| order by LastSeen desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1555.003

logsource:
    category: file_access

detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'

level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Cl0p Affiliates Target Internet-Exposed PTC Windchill and FlexPLM with Unauthenticated RCE

The Hacker News
2026-07-25 17 use cases 7 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Threat actors linked to the Cl0p (aka Chubby Scorpius, FIN11, Graceful Spider, and Lace Tempest) ransomware campaign are exploiting flaws in internet-exposed PTC Windmill and FlexPLM deployments as part of a new data extortion campaign. "Attackers chain a pre-authentication information disclosure in the FlexPLM WSDL endpoint with a server-side flaw in the Windchill login servlet, enabling

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] PTC Windchill Java/Tomcat web tier spawning OS command shell (web shell RCE) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Cl0p hex-named JSP web shell dropped under /Windchill/login/ (CVE-2026-12569) · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network connections to Cl0p CVE-2026-12569 C2 / staging infrastructure · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Windchill filesystem-enumeration artifact flst.txt written by web tier (CVE-2026-12569 discovery) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Cl0p hex-named JSP web shell dropped under /Windchill/login/ (CVE-2026-12569) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for creation of hex-named JSP web shells in the PTC Windchill/FlexPLM login directory, the post-exploitation payload of CVE-2026-12569 unauthenticated deserialization RCE. Files follow the pattern /Windchill/login/[0-9a-f]{16}.jsp and are written by the Java/Tomcat web tier — never a legitimate operation. Rationale: Uses the article's exact web-shell path /Windchill/login/ and the corroborated [0-9a-f]{16}.jsp naming pattern plus the published SHA256 — a JSP file created in the login directory has no legitimate cause, making this near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://ransom-isac.org/blog/clop-windchill-flexplm-exploitation/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/29/ptc-windchill-cve-2026-12569-exploited/ • https://www.ptc.com/en/about/trust-center/advisory-center/active-advisories/windchill-flexplm-rce-vulnerability • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/clop-ransomware-targets-windchill-flexplm-in-data-theft-attacks/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Windchill patch/hotfix deployment adding new JSP files to the web app (but not under login/ with hex names)
  • Windchill build/deploy pipeline unpacking WAR files into the app directory
  • Security scanner or IR tooling writing test .jsp files during a pentest of the PLM server
  • Backup/restore of the Windchill webapps tree re-creating existing JSP files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","tomcat9.exe","tomcat10.exe","tomcat.exe","w3wp.exe") or FileName matches regex @"^[0-9a-f]{16}\.jsp$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: retrieve the JSP file at the flagged path and hash it; compare to 55a1eb4c...; open the file — Cl0p shells contain runtime command-exec logic (Runtime.exec/ProcessBuilder). Confirm the writing process is java/tomcat. 2) Contain: isolate the Windchill/FlexPLM host from the network, preserve the web shell for forensics, and confirm CVE-2026-12569 patch (PTC June 2026 fix) is applied; rotate any service/DB credentials reachable from the app. 3) Hunt: pull Tomcat access logs for POSTs to the FlexPLM WSDL endpoint and /Windchill/login servlet from the 4 Cl0p IPs; search all Windchill hosts for additional hex-named JSPs and flst.txt enumeration output.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName endswith ".jsp"
| where FolderPath has @"\Windchill\login\" or FolderPath contains "/Windchill/login/"
| where FileName matches regex @"^[0-9a-f]{16}\.jsp$" or SHA256 == "55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".jsp"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Windchill\login\" or TargetFilePath contains "/Windchill/login/"
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"^[0-9a-f]{16}\.jsp$" or TargetFileSHA256 == "55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Cl0p Hex-Named JSP Web Shell in PTC Windchill Login Directory
id: 6f3d2a1c-9b7e-4c2a-8f11-2d4e6a7b9c01
description: Detects creation of hex-named JSP web shells under /Windchill/login/ following CVE-2026-12569 exploitation by Cl0p affiliates

PTC Windchill Java/Tomcat web tier spawning OS command shell (web shell RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE execution stage of CVE-2026-12569: the Windchill Java/Tomcat process spawning cmd/powershell/whoami/net and other discovery binaries via the deployed JSP web shell. A PLM application server should never spawn interactive OS command interpreters. Rationale: Ties the article's Windchill RCE to its concrete host behaviour: the Java/Tomcat web tier (confirmed exploited process) spawning command shells is the observable of 'remote command execution' via the JSP shell — a PLM app server has no legitimate reason to launch cmd/whoami/net. Cross-checked against: • https://ransom-isac.org/blog/clop-windchill-flexplm-exploitation/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/29/ptc-windchill-cve-2026-12569-exploited/ • https://www.securityweek.com/first-ever-exploitation-of-ptc-windchill-vulnerability-discovered-in-the-wild/
ATT&CKT1059.003 T1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windchill scheduled tasks or method-server jobs legitimately shelling out to run configured scripts (net use for file shares, hostname checks)
  • Administrator running diagnostic scripts under the Tomcat service account
  • Windchill installer/upgrade invoking cmd.exe to set environment or register services
  • Monitoring agents launched by the JVM that call ipconfig/hostname for inventory
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("WindchillDS","wt.method","windchill start","windchill stop") and AccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "Windchill")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — enumeration (whoami/net group/systeminfo) or download (certutil/bitsadmin) from the Tomcat account is high-confidence RCE; capture the parent Java command line and Windchill install path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the offending process tree, and block outbound to the 4 Cl0p IPs at the perimeter; freeze the Tomcat service account. 3) Hunt: correlate to hex-named JSP creation (UC1) and flst.txt writes on the same host in the preceding minutes; sweep peer PLM servers for identical java→cmd parentage.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","tomcat9.exe","tomcat10.exe","tomcat.exe","java")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","systeminfo.exe","ipconfig.exe","hostname.exe","tasklist.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","sh","bash","whoami","id")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("java.exe","javaw.exe","tomcat9.exe","tomcat10.exe","tomcat.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","systeminfo.exe","ipconfig.exe","hostname.exe","tasklist.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Network connections to Cl0p CVE-2026-12569 C2 / staging infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Flags any host communicating with the four Ransom-ISAC/PTC-published Cl0p IPs used to exploit and exfiltrate from Windchill/FlexPLM, with 5.180.41.35 prioritised as confirmed C2/staging. Catches inbound exploitation source IPs and outbound data-staging egress from the PLM DMZ. Rationale: Uses the four IPs jointly confirmed by Ransom-ISAC and the PTC advisory; 5.180.41.35 is flagged by Ransom-ISAC as priority-block C2/staging, so any match on a PLM host is high-fidelity regardless of direction. Cross-checked against: • https://ransom-isac.org/blog/clop-windchill-flexplm-exploitation/ • https://www.ptc.com/en/about/trust-center/advisory-center/active-advisories/windchill-flexplm-rce-vulnerability • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/clop-ransomware-targets-windchill-flexplm-in-data-theft-attacks/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sinkhole scanners in your own estate probing the same IPs
  • Security researcher or IR team validating the IOCs from a corporate egress point
  • IP reassignment — Cl0p infrastructure taken down and the address later re-leased to a benign host
  • Perimeter proxy logging a blocked connection that never completed (still worth reviewing)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal host and the initiating process; if it is the Windchill/Tomcat server or the connection is inbound to the PLM login/WSDL ports, treat as active exploitation. 2) Contain: block all four IPs at firewall/proxy, isolate any Windchill host that talked to them, and capture NetFlow bytes_out to estimate exfil volume to 5.180.41.35. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host to UC1 (web shell) and UC2 (java→cmd) events; review Tomcat access logs for the source IPs hitting the FlexPLM WSDL endpoint; scope other externally-exposed PLM assets.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("216.152.148.54","216.152.151.204","104.243.35.63","5.180.41.35")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let iocs = dynamic(["216.152.148.54","216.152.151.204","104.243.35.63","5.180.41.35"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in (iocs) or SourceIP in (iocs)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourcePort, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceAction, ApplicationProtocol, SentBytes, ReceivedBytes, RequestURL
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Windchill filesystem-enumeration artifact flst.txt written by web tier (CVE-2026-12569 discovery) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts creation of the flst.txt filesystem-enumeration output file that Cl0p affiliates generate post-exploitation on Windchill/FlexPLM servers to stage engineering/design data for theft. High fidelity when written by the Java/Tomcat web tier or a shell it spawned, or when it lands under the Windchill install tree. Rationale: flst.txt is the specific enumeration-output filename attributed to this campaign by Ransom-ISAC; scoping the writer to the Java/Tomcat web tier or the Windchill path removes generic flst.txt noise and pins it to the exploited PLM server. Cross-checked against: • https://ransom-isac.org/blog/clop-windchill-flexplm-exploitation/ • https://gbhackers.com/cl0p-targets-internet-exposed-windchill/
ATT&CKT1083 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer or admin coincidentally naming a legitimate file listing flst.txt on the server
  • Windchill batch/report jobs that emit a text file listing under the install directory
  • Backup or file-integrity tooling that produces per-directory listings named flst.txt
  • Third-party CAD/PLM integration script writing an inventory file with the same name
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" and (FolderPath has @"\Windchill\" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","tomcat9.exe","tomcat10.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open flst.txt — a recursive listing of engineering/design directories written by the Tomcat account confirms Cl0p staging; note the enumerated paths (they reveal the intended exfil target set). 2) Contain: isolate the host, preserve flst.txt and any adjacent staged archives, and revoke the Tomcat service account's access to file shares referenced in the listing. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1/UC2 on the same host and with outbound bytes to the Cl0p IPs (UC3); search all PLM servers for flst.txt and for large archive files created shortly after by the same process.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "flst.txt"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","tomcat9.exe","tomcat10.exe","tomcat.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
    or FolderPath has @"\Windchill\" or FolderPath contains "/Windchill/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "flst.txt"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("java.exe","javaw.exe","tomcat9.exe","tomcat10.exe","tomcat.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
    or TargetFilePath has @"\Windchill\" or TargetFilePath contains "/Windchill/"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1555.003

logsource:
    category: file_access

            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'

            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'

    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-12569")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-12569")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents

| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |

    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c") or SHA1 in~ ("55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c") or MD5 in~ ("55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c") or SHA1 in~ ("55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c") or MD5 in~ ("55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DevMan RaaS Portal Centralizes Payload Builds, Victim Management, and Affiliate Payouts

The Hacker News
2026-07-25 15 use cases 7 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

The operators of the DevMan ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) scheme are maintaining a dedicated web platform that offers affiliates the ability to build payloads, oversee earnings, and manage various aspects related to victims. Swiss cybersecurity company PRODAFT is tracking the centrally administered RaaS operation under the name Funky Mantis. "The portal combined build generation, finance,

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1195.002 T1486 T1528 T1555.003 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] DevMan/Funky Mantis locker execution by known SHA256/MD5 hash · Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] DevMan ransomware encryption artifacts: .devman extension and deterministic ransom note · [LLM] DevMan pre-encryption recovery inhibition and event-log clearing · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
DevMan/Funky Mantis locker execution by known SHA256/MD5 hash AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution of the DevMan (DragonForce-lineage) ransomware payload by the specific SHA256/MD5 hashes published by PRODAFT. Because DevMan is deployed hands-on-keyboard after broker access, any host running these binaries is an active encryption event, not a test. Rationale: Uses the two SHA256 and one MD5 hash published by PRODAFT for the DevMan locker; a hash match on process execution is unambiguous for an actively-deployed RaaS payload. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/prodaft/malware-ioc • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/devman-ransomware-analysis/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.devman
ATT&CKT1486 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis sandbox / detonation VM intentionally running the sample
  • IR or red-team retained sample copied to a jump box for reverse engineering
  • EDR test/validation exercise seeding known-bad hashes
  • Threat-intel researcher workstation with sample repository indexed by AV
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("SANDBOX","MALLAB","ANALYSIS"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is production (not a sandbox/analysis VM) and pull parent process + logon session for the hash hit — identify how the binary landed. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host immediately, kill the process, and disable the executing account; DevMan is hands-on-keyboard so treat as live encryption. 3) Hunt: sweep for the `.devman` extension and ransom note `e47qfsnz2trbkhnt.devman` across shares, check for VPN logins by service/backup accounts, and look for the same hashes staged on other hosts via SMB.

| where SHA256 in~ ("df5ab9015833023a03f92a797e20196672c1d6525501a9f9a94a45b0904c7403","018494565257ef2b6a4e68f1c3e7573b87fc53bd5828c9c5127f31d37ea964f8")
    or MD5 =~ "e84270afa3030b48dc9e0c53a35c65aa"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in~ ("df5ab9015833023a03f92a797e20196672c1d6525501a9f9a94a45b0904c7403","018494565257ef2b6a4e68f1c3e7573b87fc53bd5828c9c5127f31d37ea964f8")
    or MD5 =~ "e84270afa3030b48dc9e0c53a35c65aa"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DevMan ransomware encryption artifacts: .devman extension and deterministic ransom note AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts mass creation/rename of files with the DevMan-specific `.devman` extension and the builder-flaw ransom note filename `e47qfsnz2trbkhnt.devman`. Thresholding on volume per host in a short window distinguishes encryption from a one-off file. Rationale: The `.devman` extension and the deterministic note name `e47qfsnz2trbkhnt.devman` (builder flaw that re-encrypts its own notes) are DevMan-specific and independently confirmed by ANY.RUN and Malpedia; volume threshold separates encryption from noise. Cross-checked against: • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/devman-ransomware-analysis/ • https://medium.com/@anyrun/devman-ransomware-overview-32600d4da684 • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.devman
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user or app legitimately creating a file that coincidentally ends in .devman (extremely rare, non-threshold branch mitigates)
  • Backup/restore tooling replaying previously-encrypted .devman files during a recovery drill
  • EDR retro-scan re-indexing an old encrypted directory generating burst file events
  • Security team detonating a sample in a monitored share
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","wbengine.exe","backup.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the >50-file burst is on a production endpoint/share and identify the InitiatingProcess writing the `.devman` files. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the writing process, revoke the account, and disconnect mapped drives/SMB sessions to stop lateral encryption. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts touching the same share, check for the known payload hashes, event-log clearing and shadow-copy deletion (see companion UC), and service/backup-account VPN logins that likely delivered access.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".devman"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(FolderPath), Note = countif(FileName =~ "e47qfsnz2trbkhnt.devman"), Proc = any(InitiatingProcessFileName), Cmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where FileCount > 50 or Note > 0    // >50 encrypted files in 5m OR the deterministic ransom note appears
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".devman"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(TargetFilePath), Note = countif(TargetFileName =~ "e47qfsnz2trbkhnt.devman"), Proc = any(ActingProcessName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where FileCount > 50 or Note > 0
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: DevMan Ransomware Deterministic Ransom Note File Creation

DevMan pre-encryption recovery inhibition and event-log clearing AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the DevMan/DragonForce-lineage defense-evasion and recovery-inhibition chain: shadow-copy deletion via vssadmin/wmic, boot recovery disable via bcdedit, and Windows event-log clearing via wevtutil. The article explicitly enumerates recovery inhibition and event-log clearing as locker functions. Rationale: Article explicitly lists recovery inhibition and event-log clearing as DevMan Windows locker functions; the exact commands (vssadmin delete shadows, wmic shadowcopy delete, wevtutil cl, bcdedit) are corroborated as DragonForce-lineage TTPs by Picus/Intel471/SOCPrime. Cross-checked against: • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/dragonforce-ransomware-attacks-retail-giants • https://www.intel471.com/blog/dragonforce-ransomware • https://socprime.com/active-threats/ransomware-inside-dragonforces-cartel-ambitions/
ATT&CKT1490 T1070.001 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam/backup pre-snapshot shadow-copy lifecycle cleanup
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting VSS storage exhaustion with vssadmin delete shadows
  • Log-management or compliance tooling clearing event logs on a schedule via wevtutil
  • bcdedit boot-config changes during OS imaging/patching
  • DISM/servicing operations touching recovery settings
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","vsnapvss.exe","dism.exe","trustedinstaller.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("services.exe","svchost.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the command ran under a non-machine user account and whether it's part of a known backup/imaging window; pull the parent process — a scripting/ransomware parent (cmd/powershell spawned by an unusual binary) is high-signal. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host, snapshot memory, and freeze the account; expect encryption to follow within minutes. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same host and mapped shares for `.devman` files, the known payload hashes, and SMB share enumeration; correlate with recent VPN logins by service/backup accounts flagged in the PRODAFT advisory.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("delete","shadows"))
    or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("shadowcopy","delete"))
    or (FileName =~ "wevtutil.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "cl ")
    or (FileName =~ "bcdedit.exe" and (ProcessCommandLine has "recoveryenabled" or ProcessCommandLine has "ignoreallfailures"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("vssadmin.exe","wmic.exe","wevtutil.exe","bcdedit.exe")
| where (NewProcessName endswith "vssadmin.exe" and CommandLine has_all ("delete","shadows"))
    or (NewProcessName endswith "wmic.exe" and CommandLine has_all ("shadowcopy","delete"))
    or (NewProcessName endswith "wevtutil.exe" and CommandLine has "cl ")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "bcdedit.exe" and (CommandLine has "recoveryenabled" or CommandLine has "ignoreallfailures"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
